wine.name: La Faraona
wine.sites: A tiny, steep plot high on the slopes above Corullón, facing south east on slate and quartzite, its old vines farmed biodynamically like the rest of the house's.
wine.making: Fermented with native yeasts in a single open oak vat, with a share of whole bunches that the vintage decides, and left on its skins for weeks; it is then aged in barrels and larger casks of several sizes, few of them new, for some eight months to a year, the time and the vessel changing with the vintage.
wine.glass: Violet and rose petal over wild raspberry, red cherry and wet slate, with a hint of black pepper and dried herbs; pale for its depth, taut and fresh, with fine, close grained tannin and a long, stony finish.
wine.ageing: Taut and closed when young, it gains perfume with several years in bottle and is built to keep well beyond a decade in a cool cellar.
wine.serve: 15 to 17 degrees Celsius; decant a young bottle an hour ahead to open its perfume; a large Burgundy glass.

records.table: La Faraona is the high single plot at the head of Descendientes de J. Palacios's range at Corullón: old Mencía on slate, fermented with some whole bunches and aged mostly in used wood. Pale, perfumed and taut, it wants a Burgundy glass and a little air.
records.story: The house is named for the descendants of J. Palacios, patriarch of a family of wine growers in Rioja. Late in the 1990s one of his sons, already making wine in Priorat, and that son's nephew came to Bierzo in search of old Mencía on ground hard to reach and slow to yield, and settled on the steep slate around Corullón, on the western edge of the basin. They made their first wine in 1999. In 2001 they chose to bottle a few plots on their own, Las Lamas, Moncerbal, San Martín and one high above the village that became La Faraona. Around them the house built a ladder in the Burgundian manner: Pétalos del Bierzo as the regional wine, Villa de Corullón from the village and the named sites above it, with the vines farmed biodynamically. The denomination later wrote such a ladder into its own rules, and when it did the Consejo foresaw the first Viña Clasificada wines no earlier than 2025 and the first Gran Viña Clasificada no earlier than 2030. La Faraona shows a sommelier what one high plot of old Mencía can give: perfume and tension rather than weight.

report: Searches for this record: 10 of the group's share of 35, beside three the group shared on the denomination's rules; one fetch was tried (rarewineco.com, refused) and never retried, so the importer's article and sheet were read through search alone, and the south east aspect on slate is borne out by a second merchant's sheet (Vino.com, morning sun at 950 metres).

The plan's note is answered by leaving classification empty: no source read gives La Faraona a rank of the denomination's ladder, one merchant's page calls it a Gran Vinya Classificada (Priorat's Catalan term) and one news item of 2026 a viña clasificada, while the Consejo's own page foresaw the first Viña Clasificada wines no earlier than 2025 and the first Gran Viña Clasificada no earlier than 2030.

Founded is the library's 1999 and the first wine of 1999 rests on the importer's sheet and article; one importer's sheet gives the company as established in 1998, and the first separate bottling of La Faraona in 2001 rests on the importer's article and Spanish Wine Lover.

The plot's altitude is about 855 metres on the importer's sheet, more than 800, 900 and 950 in merchants' listings and about 975 or nearly 1,000 in others, so the record says near the upper limit of the vine; the paraje is named El Fierro, El Ferro and El Ferrol in three listings and one sheet places it on a tectonic fault, so neither the name nor the fault is given.

The ageing is nine to ten months in barrel for the 2019 (Berry Bros.), twelve in foudre and barrique for the 2018, six and a half in one shop's sheet and fifteen to eighteen months for the house's wines above Pétalos in an older Spanish Wine Lover article, hence the range; the whole bunch share is 10 to 50 per cent by vintage (Spanish Wine Lover) and over 30 per cent on the importer's sheet, with 0 to 30 per cent new wood and maceration of 45 to 90 days in one oak vat.

Left out for want of a second source tied to a listed page: the patriarch's death in 2000 (in several accounts read through search), the origin of the name La Faraona, the vines' age (seventy and more, and eighty two, in two listings) and any horses or mules in the vineyards.
The library's w-la-faraona calls the wine the summit of Bierzo's classified ladder; that reads true of the house's own ladder, but no source read gives it a rank of the denomination's.
Living names met, none in the fragment: the son and the nephew who founded the house (both on people.json); the patriarch is described, not named, since his dates were not found in two sources.

wine.name: Ultreia Saint Jacques
wine.grapes: Mencía, all or almost all of it, from old vines.
wine.sites: Old vines around Valtuille de Abajo; the house's own sheet for one vintage places the wine in the site of Villegas there.
wine.making: Fermented with a large share of whole bunches, stems and all, in open oak vats, and left on its skins for two months and more; the wine is then aged in used barrels, larger casks and cement, and bottled without fining or filtering, by the house's own sheet.
wine.glass: Red cherry, wild strawberry and blood orange over crushed slate, with a green, peppery lift from the stems and a breath of sea air; light to medium in body, juicy and fresh, with fine, slightly grainy tannin.
wine.ageing: Lively and open on release, it drinks well over its first several years and gains savoury notes of dried cherry and leaf with a few more.
wine.serve: 13 to 15 degrees Celsius, a little cool to keep it fresh; no need to decant; a Burgundy glass.

records.table: Ultreia Saint Jacques is the Raúl Pérez house's Mencía from old vines at Valtuille de Abajo, named for the greeting of the pilgrims who cross Bierzo. Made with whole bunches and aged in used wood, it is fresh, juicy and lightly peppery; pour it a little cool.
records.story: Bierzo was recognised as a denomination in 1989, and the grower behind this house comes from a family of Valtuille de Abajo whose bodega is Castro Ventosa. He learnt his trade there in the 1990s before going his own way. In 2003, by the house's own account, he began a range of his own and called it Ultreia, the Latin greeting pilgrims give one another on the road to Santiago, read as go further. That road crosses Bierzo on its way into Galicia, and Saint Jacques, the apostle at its end in French, names the Mencía drawn from old vines around Valtuille. The house works with whole bunches, long macerations in open oak vats and used wood, after perfume and freshness rather than weight. From Bierzo the grower carried the same ways west into Galicia, to Amandi in Ribeira Sacra and to Rías Baixas, so that the house's name is met across the Atlantic north west. Ultreia Saint Jacques is its wide release: the old Mencía of Valtuille, fragrant and lively, made for the table rather than the cellar.

records.table: Castro Ventosa is the family bodega of Valtuille de Abajo, and Valtuille Cepas Centenarias its Mencía from vines more than a century old. Aged about a year in used French oak, it is deep and savoury yet fresh, a red to decant an hour ahead.
records.story: The bodega takes its name from Castro Ventosa, the walled hill site between Cacabelos and Villafranca del Bierzo, long linked with Bergidum Flavium, the Roman town from which Bierzo is held to take its name; the family's cellar stands at the foot of its western slope. By the house's account the family has grown vines at Valtuille de Abajo since 1752, on plots that became part of the estate, across nine generations. It bottled its first wines in 1989, under another name, and in the 1990s gave the bodega the name of the hill. Valtuille Cepas Centenarias followed with the 1999 vintage, drawn from the family's Mencía of a century and more, with a little Garnacha Tintorera, Bastardo and white grapes among them, as the old growers planted. In 2017, as the denomination prepared its ladder of village and site wines, the house added a village wine named for Valtuille, and wines of named sites of the village sit above it. For Cepas Centenarias the cellar keeps to used French barrels, so that the old vines speak rather than the wood. For a sommelier, Cepas Centenarias shows what a century of vine age gives Mencía: depth and calm without heaviness.

report: Searches for this record: 7 of the group's share of 35, one restricted to the house's domain and the region's tourism portal; no fetch tried for this house.

The plan's note is answered: the house's own pages give the family's vines at Valtuille since 1752 across nine generations, the cellar at the foot of the western slope of the Roman site that gives it its name, Cepas Centenarias made since 1999 and the village wine Castro Ventosa Valtuille of 2017; the century old vines are given by the house's importers (Indigo Wine, Kensington) and Bodeboca.

Founded is left empty: the family dates its vines to 1752 and its first estate bottling to 1989, and the bodega took its name in 1991 (Enterwine, with a wiki entry and a second listing read through search), so no single year founds the house; one listing gives 1999, the year of Cepas Centenarias.

The field blend rests on Bodeboca's sheet for 2022 (Alicante Bouschet, which is Garnacha Tintorera, and Bastardo) and Grand Cru Wijnen's for 2023 (a single plot at Mata Los Pardos with a little Trousseau, which is Bastardo); the single plot also rests on Bodeboca's 2021 sheet, and the plot's name is left out as single sourced.

About a year in used French barrels rests on Bodeboca (twelve months, 225 and 500 litres), Vinos Cutanda and Private Cellar (eleven months) and Gourmet Hunters (twelve, unfined and unfiltered); the fermentation in a 5,000 litre foudre with native yeasts and sixty days on the skins is Bodeboca's for one vintage and is left out.

The plan's sandy valley floor is not borne out for this wine: one listing gives its soil as mostly clay, another the Villegas plot as sandy, so no soil is given; ungrafted vines rest on one importer and are left out.

The bond with Bergidum Flavium is hedged because the University of Salamanca's study says the hill has always been linked with the Roman town while the town's exact site is disputed (Castro Ventosa or La Edrada at Cacabelos); the Templar castle at Ponferrada in a question's explanation rests on general knowledge, not a listed source.

Living names met, for people.json: the grower who founded the Ultreia house and his nephew, the winemaker, of the family (see raul-perez), and the founder of another Valtuille bodega met on the tourism portal (Marcos García Alba); the grandmother named in the bodega's first name of 1989 is not named for want of dates.

records.table: Cepas Viejas is the red that launched Dominio de Tares in Bierzo Alto: Mencía from old bush vines on slate, aged some ten months in oak. Dark fruited, smooth and lightly toasted, it shows the riper, oak aged face of the grape.
records.story: Dominio de Tares was born in 2000 at San Román de Bembibre, in Bierzo Alto on the eastern side of the basin, as a house set on recovering old vineyards. Its founders, by the house's account, searched the denomination for sites on very different soils. Cepas Viejas was its first wine: a modern red, aged in oak, in which Mencía was meant to stand at the centre, made from old bush vines on slate. Beside it the house made a Godello fermented in barrel, and its sister bodega in Los Oteros of León, Dominio Dostares, took up the old Prieto Picudo vines there. The denomination itself drew up new rules, which the Ministry ratified in 2019, adding Estaladiña and Merenzao to its grapes and a ladder of village, site and classified vineyard wines. In time the house gave the name Cepas Viejas to its barrel fermented Godello as well, so that a red and a white share it. For a sommelier, Cepas Viejas stands for the Bierzo of the early 2000s: ripe Mencía from old vines, shaped by oak.

report: Searches for this record: 4 of the group's share of 35, two restricted to the house's own domains; no fetch tried for this house.

The plan's note is answered: the house's own pages give 2000 for its birth (with Spanish Wine Lover and Cellar Tours), Cepas Viejas as its first wine, Mencía alone, vines of more than eighty five years up to 700 metres on decomposed slate and, for one vintage, bush vines of more than eighty years around the Castro Bergidum, which is Castro Ventosa; the record says eighty years and more because the figure grows each year.

The Godello of the same name is kept apart in a trap and in others: the house's shop and its sheet for 2023 give wild yeasts, 500 litre barrels and about six months on the lees in French oak; the year of the renaming (2024 in the plan, a Cepas Viejas Godello 2023 sheet uploaded in 2024) is left out.

The time in oak is ten months on the house's shop and its note on the 2022, nine in one shop's listing and nine for the 2011 in the house's own news, with French and American barrels for that vintage; the American share and the eighteen months in bottle of one vintage are left out, and the record says many months in bottle.

Left out for want of a second source: the group of friends who founded the house (one retailer quoting the house), the old vineyards of forty to ninety years in three zones, the growers it buys from in Valtuille de Abajo and Villadecanes (Spanish Wine Lover alone), its claim to have pioneered aged Mencía and barrel fermented Godello, and the meaning of the name Tares; the closing line is the author's reading of the house's own words for the checker to test.
The region's producers line (one of the first serious barrel fermented Godellos) is not borne out by two sources and is not repeated; the plan's slate and clay is the house's decomposed slate.
Living names met, none in the fragment: a person interviewed for the house on Onda Madrid (Rafael Somonte, role not read), for people.json as a precaution.

wine.name: Losada
wine.grapes: Mencía, almost all of it, from old vines, with a touch of the white Doña Blanca in some vintages.
wine.sites: Old vines on the clay slopes near the cellar at Pieros, on the pilgrims' road between Cacabelos and Villafranca del Bierzo, farmed as many small plots.
wine.making: Picked by hand and made plot by plot, the wine is fermented with native yeasts in stainless steel and then aged for about a year in French oak barrels of their second and third use before bottling.
wine.glass: Black cherry and plum over liquorice, with a hint of toast and dark chocolate from the barrel and a note of wild mountain herbs; round and supple, with fresh acidity and soft, ripe tannin.
wine.ageing: Generous on release, it drinks well over its first five years or so and gains savoury notes with a few more.
wine.serve: 15 to 17 degrees Celsius; it needs no decanting, though a few minutes of air help; a large red wine glass.

label.means: The house's namesake red, drawn from the clay slopes near its cellar.
Estate wines: the house's name for wines grown on its own plots.
The appellation of the basin, here on the clay of the valley rather than the slate hills.

records.table: Losada is the namesake Mencía of Losada Vinos de Finca at Pieros, from old vines on the clay slopes by the pilgrims' road. Aged about a year in French oak, it is round, ripe and supple, a red to pour beside roast meats or a stew.
records.story: Losada Vinos de Finca began in the middle of the 2000s, in 2004 or 2005 by different accounts, with small plots of old Mencía around Pieros, a hamlet on the pilgrims' road between Cacabelos and Villafranca del Bierzo, and the village of Valtuille. Where other newcomers sought slate, it went looking for old Mencía on soils rich in clay, worked as many small plots rather than one estate. The namesake Losada is drawn from the clay slopes close to the cellar. Above it the range climbs to Altos de Losada, from old plots at Valtuille de Arriba aged in concrete eggs, large casks and barrels, and to La Bienquerida, a Vino de Paraje from an old plot at Las Chas that the house brought back after long neglect. From 2017, by its own account, the house sowed cover crops, returned to the plough and replanted vines, grafting them to Mencía. Bierzo is often taught through its slate, and Losada is the other half of the lesson. For a sommelier, the namesake wine is the softer side of Mencía: round and generous from clay, beside the taut reds of the slate hills, and an easy first bottle of the valley at the table.

report: Searches for this record: 4 of the group's share of 35, one restricted to the house's domain; no fetch tried for this house.

The plan's note is answered: founded is left empty because Enterwine, Spanish Wine Lover and an interview of 2011 give 2005 and Wine Spies and another listing 2004, and the story gives both; the label is Losada with Bierzo on the house's page.

La Bienquerida's Vino de Paraje of Las Chas from 2018 rests on Bodeboca alone (in two languages), and no page of the Consejo read names it, so the record calls it a single plot at Las Chas and gives no rank; Bodeboca's planting of 1906 on slate and Enterwine's Las Chas at Valtuille de Abajo against the house's distributor's Valtuille de Arriba are left out.

The house's product page gives twelve months in French oak barrels for Losada and its Guía Gourmets notice of 2025 twelve months between concrete eggs and barrels with a touch of Doña Blanca; the record follows the product page, and the notice is not listed because its title carries a judgement.

Left out for want of a second source: the cellar opposite the hill of Castro Ventosa and its year (about 2009 by Alimarket), the shared shareholders and management with Bodegas Valdesil of Valdeorras by Alimarket in 2009, the local word piezas for the plots and the founders' story of a prophecy fulfilled (Enterwine alone).

Living names met, for people.json: the winemaker named on the house's page and in an interview address (Amancio Fernández Gómez) and the architect of the cellar (Jesús Manzanares, status not read, as a precaution); the house's page on the winemaker's training is not used because it would describe a present role.
